examples.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $x^{2}+16x+k=0$ has two distinct real solutions.
examples.solution_text:
$a=1,\ b=16,\ c=k$.
$\begin{align*}\Delta&=16^{2}-4(1)(k)\\&=256-4k\end{align*}$
For two distinct real solutions, $\Delta>0$.
$\begin{align*}256-4k&>0\\-4k&>-256\\k&<64\end{align*}$
Dividing by $-4$ reverses the inequality.

examples.question_text: Find the value of $k$ for which $3x^{2}-18x+k=0$ has exactly one real solution.
examples.solution_text:
$a=3,\ b=-18,\ c=k$.
$\begin{align*}\Delta&=(-18)^{2}-4(3)(k)\\&=324-12k\end{align*}$
For exactly one real solution, $\Delta=0$.
$\begin{align*}324-12k&=0\\12k&=324\\k&=27\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $x^{2}+k=18x$ has no real solutions.
examples.solution_text:
Write the equation in standard form.
$x^{2}-18x+k=0$
$a=1,\ b=-18,\ c=k$.
$\begin{align*}\Delta&=(-18)^{2}-4(1)(k)\\&=324-4k\end{align*}$
For no real solutions, $\Delta<0$.
$\begin{align*}324-4k&<0\\-4k&<-324\\k&>81\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $x^{2}+kx+36=0$ has exactly one real solution.
examples.solution_text:
$a=1,\ b=k,\ c=36$.
$\begin{align*}\Delta&=k^{2}-4(1)(36)\\&=k^{2}-144\end{align*}$
For exactly one real solution, $\Delta=0$.
$\begin{align*}k^{2}-144&=0\\k^{2}&=144\\k&=\pm12\end{align*}$
Both parameter values give a repeated real root.

examples.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $3x^{2}+kx+3=0$ has no real solutions.
examples.solution_text:
$a=3,\ b=k,\ c=3$.
$\begin{align*}\Delta&=k^{2}-4(3)(3)\\&=k^{2}-36\end{align*}$
For no real solutions, $\Delta<0$.
$\begin{align*}k^{2}-36&<0\\k^{2}&<36\end{align*}$
The square of $k$ is less than $36$ precisely when $k$ lies between $-6$ and $6$.
$-6<k<6$

examples.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $(k+3)x^{2}+2x-2=0$ has two distinct real solutions.
examples.solution_text:
The equation is quadratic when $k\ne-3$.
$a=k+3,\ b=2,\ c=-2$.
$\begin{align*}\Delta&=2^{2}-4(k+3)(-2)\\&=4+8(k+3)\\&=8k+28\end{align*}$
For two distinct real solutions, $\Delta>0$.
$\begin{align*}8k+28&>0\\8k&>-28\\k&>-\frac{7}{2}\end{align*}$
When $k=-3$, the original equation becomes $2x-2=0$, with only one real solution, $x=1$.
Therefore $k>-\frac{7}{2}$ and $k\ne-3$.

examples.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $kx^{2}-10x+k=0$ has exactly one real solution, given $k\ne0$.
examples.solution_text:
$a=k,\ b=-10,\ c=k$.
$\begin{align*}\Delta&=(-10)^{2}-4(k)(k)\\&=100-4k^{2}\end{align*}$
For exactly one real solution, $\Delta=0$.
$\begin{align*}100-4k^{2}&=0\\4k^{2}&=100\\k^{2}&=25\\k&=\pm5\end{align*}$
Both values satisfy $k\ne0$.

examples.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $x^{2}-(k+3)x+25=0$ has exactly one real solution.
examples.solution_text:
$a=1,\ b=-(k+3),\ c=25$.
$\begin{align*}\Delta&=(-(k+3))^{2}-4(1)(25)\\&=(k+3)^{2}-100\end{align*}$
For exactly one real solution, $\Delta=0$.
$\begin{align*}(k+3)^{2}-100&=0\\(k+3)^{2}&=100\\k+3&=\pm10\end{align*}$
Thus $k=7$ or $k=-13$.

examples.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $kx^{2}-(2k-3)x+k=0$ has no real solutions, given $k\ne0$.
examples.solution_text:
$a=k,\ b=-(2k-3),\ c=k$.
$\begin{align*}\Delta&=(-(2k-3))^{2}-4(k)(k)\\&=4k^{2}-12k+9-4k^{2}\\&=9-12k\end{align*}$
For no real solutions, $\Delta<0$.
$\begin{align*}9-12k&<0\\-12k&<-9\\k&>\frac{3}{4}\end{align*}$
Every value in this range satisfies $k\ne0$.

coverage.summary: Authored nine examples covering the distinct accepted assessment methods, using changed values and supplied booklet teaching. The interval example combines the booklet's negative-discriminant condition with its parameter-in-b question type. Solutions use editable prose and single-dollar aligned mathematics; blue ink is supplied by the renderer. No diagrams are needed for these algebraic tasks. Practice and quiz mathematics were neither changed nor re-audited. Independent example review and actual visual capture remain pending.

examples.derivation: Δ=16²−4k=256−4k. Two distinct real solutions require 256−4k>0, giving k<64.
Δ=(−18)²−4(3)k=324−12k. Setting Δ=0 gives k=27; the equation becomes 3(x−3)²=0.
Standard form is x²−18x+k=0. Δ=324−4k<0 gives k>81.
Δ=k²−144=0 gives k=±12. The corresponding equations are (x+6)²=0 and (x−6)²=0.
Δ=k²−36<0 gives k²<36, hence −6<k<6. This combines the supplied negative-discriminant condition with the parameter-in-b type, preserving the accepted interval assessment method.
For k≠−3, Δ=4+8(k+3)=8k+28>0 gives k>−7/2. At k=−3, the original equation is 2x−2=0 with one solution, so exclude −3.
Δ=100−4k²=0 gives k²=25 and k=±5, both allowed. The equations become 5(x−1)²=0 and −5(x+1)²=0.
Δ=(k+3)²−100=0 gives k+3=±10, hence k=7 or −13. These yield (x−5)²=0 and (x+5)²=0.
Δ=(2k−3)²−4k²=9−12k. The condition Δ<0 gives k>3/4, which automatically satisfies k≠0.
